description: Human-readable detail per obligation: context (what it is), implications for US beverages, the action, the governing CFR or equivalent, and backlinks. Keyed by obligation_id from regwatch-obligations.csv. Authored for internal research; confirm against primary text before any compliance or marketing use.

us-fed-gras-overhaul.what: GRAS (Generally Recognized As Safe) is the status that lets a substance be added to food without FDA premarket approval if qualified experts agree it is safe. For decades a company could self-affirm GRAS and never tell FDA. FDA has signaled it will close that self-affirmation path and is re-reviewing older additives, several of which appear in beverages.
us-fed-gras-overhaul.means: Any ingredient a beverage relies on under self-affirmed GRAS now needs a clean, audit-ready safety dossier. Preservatives such as BHA and BHT are early federal re-review targets. If FDA narrows the GRAS pathway, ingredients in use today could require a notification or a reformulation.
us-fed-gras-overhaul.action: Inventory every self-affirmed GRAS ingredient in the portfolio and assemble its safety file now; flag any on FDA's re-review list for a reformulation contingency.

backlinks.label: FDA: How U.S. FDA's GRAS Notification Program Works

us-fed-dye-phaseout.what: Certified color additives are the synthetic FD&C dyes (Red 40, Yellow 5, Yellow 6, Blue 1, Blue 2, Green 3) listed and batch-certified by FDA. In 2025 FDA and HHS announced a push to phase out petroleum-based dyes, and FDA had already revoked the authorization for FD&C Red No. 3 in food in January 2025.
us-fed-dye-phaseout.means: Flavored and colored sparkling drinks that use certified dyes face reformulation pressure to exempt-from-certification colors (fruit, vegetable, and mineral sources under 21 CFR Part 73). A color change is also a claims event: it can support or undercut a 'no artificial colors' statement, so it must route through claims review, not just R&D.
us-fed-dye-phaseout.action: Map every SKU's color source. For any certified dye, plan a Part 73 alternative and coordinate the label/claims change. Treat the Red No. 3 food deauthorization as a hard removal item for any affected formula.

us-fed-upf-definition.what: There is no legal definition of 'ultra-processed food' yet. FDA and USDA announced they are jointly developing one. There is no CFR text today; this is a watch item that, once defined, becomes a lever for warnings, school restrictions, and marketing pressure.
us-fed-upf-definition.means: Sweetened and heavily formulated beverages are likely to land inside whatever definition emerges, especially products using non-nutritive sweeteners. It is not an immediate deadline but it shapes the medium-term reformulation and positioning strategy.
us-fed-upf-definition.action: Track the joint FDA/USDA definition work; pressure-test the portfolio against the leading candidate definitions so a position is ready when text appears.

us-fed-fop-labeling.what: FDA proposed a front-of-package nutrition label (a 'Nutrition Info' box) that would rate Saturated Fat, Sodium, and Added Sugars as Low, Medium, or High on the front panel. It amends the food-labeling regulations in 21 CFR Part 101.
us-fed-fop-labeling.means: For a sweetened drink, added sugar is the most likely 'High' trigger and would reshape the front panel. A zero-sugar line is comparatively well positioned, but any reformulation or redesign should be coordinated with this rule so the front panel is changed once, not twice.
us-fed-fop-labeling.action: Model each SKU against the proposed thresholds; sequence any front-panel redesign to absorb the FOP box in a single coordinated change.

us-fed-healthy-claim-rule.what: FDA's updated 'healthy' claim rule redefines when a food may be labeled 'healthy': it must fit a food-group model, not just hit nutrient thresholds. The final rule is codified at 21 CFR 101.65; it was effective in 2025 with a compliance date in 2028.
us-fed-healthy-claim-rule.means: Adding vitamins to an unhealthy base no longer rescues a 'healthy' claim. Any beverage that carries or implies 'healthy' must be re-checked against the new definition before the compliance date.
us-fed-healthy-claim-rule.action: Audit every product that uses or implies 'healthy' against 21 CFR 101.65 and remove or substantiate the claim before the 2028 compliance date.

backlinks.label: FDA: Use of the Term Healthy on Food Labeling

us-fed-caffeine-guidance.what: Caffeine added to cola-type beverages is GRAS up to 0.02 percent under 21 CFR 182.1180. FDA has separately warned about pure and highly concentrated caffeine and is working on voluntary caffeine-labeling guidance for the energy and functional categories.
us-fed-caffeine-guidance.means: A caffeinated line must keep added caffeine within the GRAS basis for its category and be ready for voluntary labeling expectations. Energy positioning also intersects Canada's supplemented-foods caution statements.
us-fed-caffeine-guidance.action: Confirm per-serving caffeine against the GRAS basis for the product category and prepare cautionary-statement copy for markets that expect it.

backlinks.label: FDA: Spilling the Beans on Caffeine

us-ca-ab418.what: California AB 418, the California Food Safety Act, bans the manufacture or sale in California of foods containing brominated vegetable oil, potassium bromate, propylparaben, or FD&C Red No. 3, effective January 1, 2027. It is state law, not FDA, but it parallels federal action: FDA revoked BVO's food authorization in 2024 and Red No. 3's food authorization in 2025.
us-ca-ab418.means: BVO and Red No. 3 are the concrete near-term beverage items. Any formula sold in California containing either must be out before January 1, 2027, and the federal revocations make removal a national, not just California, question.
us-ca-ab418.action: Confirm with R&D and suppliers that no California-sold formula contains the four banned substances; treat BVO and Red No. 3 as national removal items given the parallel federal revocations.

cfr.citation: Federal parallel: BVO authorization revoked (former 21 CFR 180.30)
Federal parallel: FD&C Red No. 3 (21 CFR Part 74)

us-ca-prop65.what: Proposition 65 is California's 1986 right-to-know law. It does not ban anything; it requires a warning when a product exposes a person to one of roughly 1,000 listed chemicals above a safe-harbor level. For beverages the drivers are trace heavy metals (lead, cadmium, arsenic, mercury) and acrylamide carried in by botanicals, colors, concentrates, or water.
us-ca-prop65.means: Exposure, not harm, triggers a private enforcer's notice, and the burden shifts to the company to prove the exposure is below the safe-harbor level. Bottled water and botanical or fruit-forward beverages carry the most realistic heavy-metal exposure.
us-ca-prop65.action: Maintain annual heavy-metal and acrylamide testing for California-sold products, secure supplier attestation and indemnity, and apply warnings where a safe-harbor level cannot be met.

ca-fed-supplemented-foods.what: Health Canada's Supplemented Foods Regulations govern foods with added supplemental ingredients (including caffeine and certain vitamins). They require a Supplemented Food Facts table, cautionary statements, and caffeine limits, under Canada's Food and Drug Regulations rather than the US CFR.
ca-fed-supplemented-foods.means: A caffeinated or functional beverage sold in Canada may need cautionary statements and must stay within Canadian caffeine limits, which can differ from the US GRAS basis. This is the main Canadian touchpoint for the portfolio.
ca-fed-supplemented-foods.action: Map any Canada-distributed SKU to the supplemented-foods requirements: caffeine limit, cautionary statements, and the Supplemented Food Facts table.

mx-fed-nom051.what: Mexico's NOM-051 front-of-pack labeling requires black octagon warning seals for products high in calories, sugars, saturated fat, or sodium, plus disclaimer legends when a product contains non-nutritive sweeteners or added caffeine. It is Mexican federal law published in the Diario Oficial de la Federacion, not US CFR.
mx-fed-nom051.means: A sweetened or non-nutritive-sweetened beverage sold in Mexico likely carries one or more octagon seals and a sweetener disclaimer, and products with those seals face marketing-to-children restrictions. It is the strictest front-of-pack regime the portfolio meets.
mx-fed-nom051.action: For Mexico-distributed SKUs, determine the octagon seals and sweetener/caffeine legends triggered and confirm packaging compliance.
